name: Gareth Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential. What is your usual day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and manage seven reservations staff for a large hotel company that runs three properties near the old river bridge. I have done this for twelve years, know the room mix and manage the team competently, though I still ask the night clerk before changing a late arrival. My bachelor’s degree is in hospitality. I use AI every day to draft an occupancy forecast, then check the actual cancellations and ask the desk which guests are coming.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are money and work options at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Alma cooks in a school cafeteria, and our grown daughter and son live in their own homes. We rent near the hotels, my manager pay is low for the role and we have less than three weeks of expenses saved after our car repair. There are few similar reservation jobs nearby. I believe in paid apprenticeships and families helping when they can, but I would not put our children’s earnings into my budget without asking them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the desk that an occupancy forecast is useful only after someone confirms the cancellations. A guest still needs a person to explain why a prepaid room disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team should keep working, but Alma’s school kitchen has fewer hours in holidays and our cash lasts less than three weeks. My own pension access and net amount are unknown, so I cannot call this close to retirement money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d keep the morning cancellation call and compare each AI forecast with the front desk’s paid-room list. During the first year I’d ask my pension provider for an access date and net-income statement and stop the extra takeaway meal when cafeteria hours dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the rent, though the booking job stays familiar. A full screen does not pay a bill if half those rooms cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which forecast fooled you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One weekend looked full until a wedding party moved its date and the software kept their rooms in the count. The night clerk knew before my chart did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep using AI if it got that wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It saves me an hour of draft work when I check the cancellations. I use the AI forecast as a pencil, not a second front desk.

say: I’d check **real cancellations** before trusting a room forecast.
A prepaid guest needs a **human answer** when a room disappears.
think: My **reservations team** should continue in a plateau.
Alma’s **school-holiday hours** and under three weeks cash leave rent exposed.
do: Keep the **morning desk call** and check AI forecasts against paid rooms.
Request **pension figures** for access and net income; cut a takeaway meal when kitchen hours dip.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent despite familiar work.
S0.quote: I use the AI forecast as a pencil, not a second front desk.
fieldNote: He is an **experienced average manager** who uses AI every day with checks.
The household has **under three weeks cash** after a car repair.
His own pension is **unverified**, so age cannot fund rent.

steps.text: Keep morning cancellation call and compare AI forecast with front-desk paid rooms
Ask pension provider for written access date and net monthly income
Skip extra takeaway meal when Alma’s cafeteria hours dip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI can write replies, set rates and move bookings, but the desk must be able to reverse a bad move. I would let staff see a live guest’s charge before a tool changes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pricing and booking are most of my work, so the hotel might keep fewer reservations staff and combine managers. I have experience, but there are only three properties and my own post could be removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d ask the revenue director to trial AI prices on copied bookings for one quiet midweek stay, with the night clerk paid to mark wrong refunds. If the clerk and finance lead confirm the charges, I’d use it for that stay in the first year with human reversal access, and ask for written staffing dates before any posts change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about my team and my own pay. A cheaper night for a guest is no success if the hotel quietly owes the wrong person a refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would stop the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Charging a guest again after a refund was approved. The machine should not be allowed to use a clean booking code as an excuse for a double charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach the desk to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the finance lead and night clerk can show a correct refund and reversal. I would ask the company to pay their learning hours, not bury training in a late shift.

say: I’d preserve **human reversal access** for wrong guest charges.
A copied-booking trial needs **paid night-clerk checks** before live pricing.
think: Booking and pricing work could leave **fewer staff**.
Even an experienced manager could lose **my own post** in a merger.
do: Ask for a **quiet-stay price trial** on copied bookings with paid checks.
Use **AI prices** only after clerk and finance confirm charges, retaining human reversal access.
Ask for **written staffing dates** before any reservations posts change.
feel: I feel **anxious** about refunds and wages.
S1.quote: A cheaper night for a guest is no success if the hotel quietly owes the wrong person a refund.
fieldNote: His AI enthusiasm still depends on **refund accuracy**.
He names his own **merger risk** despite experience.
Paid staff learning hours are a **condition he requests**, not yet a company promise.

steps.text: Ask revenue director to trial one quiet stay with paid night-clerk refund checks
Use AI prices only after clerk and finance confirm charges, with human reversal access

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell guests to keep their payment confirmations and ask the hotel who answers a wrong charge. I’d ask the company for a written date and pay terms if the reservations team closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could price rooms, answer guests and handle cancellations as well as I can, so I expect my post to end near sixty. Alma’s cooking is hands-on until robots around 2031, but her term-time wage alone cannot cover rent and food; I still need my own pension figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request my provider’s written age-sixty access and net amount and ask the hotel what outside-work rules apply to paid walking tours. Before 2028 I’d ask two local inns whether they would sell a Saturday walk by the old bridge, but I would take a booking only if they and the guests agree a price, the required cover is affordable and Alma can use the car for her shifts; in the first year after AGI I’d run paid walks only with actual bookings and keep seeking posted hotel work if the walks and verified pension cannot cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. A tour is an idea I can test; it is not next month’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would visitors pay for your walk if AGI plans it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An AI can write the route and story in 2028. A guest might pay a person to show the bridge until robots can do the walking around 2031, but I will ask before counting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your adult children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them we are looking for paid work. I would not ask them to pay for a tour that has not sold a place.

say: I’d ask for **written closure terms** and a human wrong-charge contact.
Guests should keep **payment confirmations** when booking systems change.
think: I expect my **booking post** to end around sixty.
Alma’s cafeteria pay cannot cover rent and food; physical cooking follows **2031 robots**.
My own **pension income** remains unverified, so age sixty cannot fill a wage gap.
do: Request **written age-sixty pension figures** and outside-work rules.
Ask **two local inns** about paid bridge walks; take bookings only with agreed price, affordable cover and Alma’s car access.
After AGI, run **paid walks** only if booked; seek posted hotel work if walks and pension fall short.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a tour is not rent.
S2.quote: A tour is an idea I can test; it is not next month’s rent.
fieldNote: His tour is a **commercial demand test**, not promised family income.
AGI writes the **route and story** in 2028 before 2031 walking robots.
Bookings require an **agreed price**, affordable cover and car access alongside a job search.

steps.text: Request written age-sixty pension access and net-income figures and hotel outside-work rules
Ask two inns about paid bridge walks before 2028
Take paid tour bookings only with agreed prices affordable cover and Alma’s car access
Seek posted hotel work if booked walks and verified pension cannot cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell hotels five years is time to publish real jobs and teach staff on paid hours, rather than offer a leaflet about careers. A visitor should know whether a human guide has actually been booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 I may have pension access, but only a net figure can tell us if it meets rent. Walking tours still require booking and scripts, which 2031 AGI can do; the physical walk may face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d run one Saturday bridge walk a month only if a local inn prepays enough places to cover insurance, travel and my time without taking the car from Alma’s kitchen shift. Before 2031 I’d apply for a posted hotel guest-relations vacancy only if its written pay plus Alma’s actual earnings covers rent and food; after AGI I’d keep walking with guests only while they pay, knowing the booking desk and tour planning are already exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but have time to test one route honestly. I would rather cancel an empty walk than call it a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many people make a walk worth doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would add the insurance and travel cost to an hourly wage and divide it by the price the inn agrees. I cannot say a number before they quote their share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hotel job is just booking again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it faces 2031 AGI too. I would take a real paid vacancy as a bridge, not a title that promises safety.

say: I’d demand **posted hotel wages** and paid learning, not career leaflets.
Guests should know whether a **human guide** is booked.
think: My **pension at 63** needs a verified net amount.
Tour scripts and bookings face **2031 AGI** before 2034 walking robots.
do: Run **one prepaid walk monthly** only if fees cover insurance, travel, time and Alma keeps the car.
Apply for **posted guest-relations work** only with written pay plus Alma’s earnings covering rent and food.
After AGI, keep **paid human walks** only while guests book them.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can test real bookings.
S3.quote: I would rather cancel an empty walk than call it a business.
fieldNote: He uses a **net paid booking test**, not a guest-count guess.
A new hotel post remains **AGI-exposed booking work**.
Alma’s car access is a **hard condition** even for a small tour.

steps.text: Run one monthly bridge walk only after prepaid places cover insurance travel and his time
Keep car available for Alma’s kitchen shift before any Saturday tour
Apply for posted guest-relations role only with written wages plus Alma’s earnings covering rent and food
Continue paid human tours after 2031 only while guests book them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company a decade is enough to publish staffing and pension dates for hotel workers. I would tell visitors a walking guide should be named and paid, not generated as an image on a booking page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036. My own pension might be accessible, but I need the provider’s net figure and Alma’s actual wage then before saying we can stop working; booking, tour scripts and online guest replies face 2036 AGI, while physical guiding and cafeteria cooking face robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every January from 2027 I’d ask my provider for updated access and net income and count actual net walk receipts, not reservations that can cancel. I’d keep my paid hotel role while offered and consider stopping only if verified pension plus Alma’s then-current pay covers rent, health and food; in the first year after AGI I’d continue paid bridge walks only if guests still book and cover costs, and look for posted paid work if they do not or our income is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious even with ten years. A longer calendar gives time to sell real walks, not permission to call pension money before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Alma has stopped working by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we count zero wages from her and ask whether my verified pension and paid work cover the rent. I will not use a hoped-for kitchen shift to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to run the walks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have jobs and homes of their own, and neither has asked to guide tourists. Family support is a conversation, not a business assumption.

say: I’d ask for **staffing and pension dates** before 2036.
A **named paid guide** should be real, not an image in a booking page.
think: At **68 in 2036**, pension and Alma’s then-current income must be verified.
Booking and scripts face **2036 AGI** before 2039 physical guiding robots.
do: Check **pension figures** and net walk receipts each January.
Keep **paid hotel work** while offered; consider stopping only if accessible pension plus Alma’s actual pay covers rent, health and food.
Continue **paid walks** after AGI only with bookings covering costs; seek posted work if walks fail or household income is short.
feel: I feel **anxious** because bookings do not guarantee rent.
S4.quote: I will not use a hoped-for kitchen shift to retire.
fieldNote: He never counts **unpaid reservations** as earnings.
His pension and Alma’s future wage are **separate uncertain inputs**.
Tour guide presence remains **temporary physical work** before later robots.

steps.text: Request updated pension access and net-income figures and tally net walk receipts each January
Keep paid hotel work; consider stopping only if accessible pension plus Alma’s pay covers bills
Continue paid walks after 2036 only with bookings covering costs
Seek posted paid work if walks fail or verified household income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the bookings desk could close before I have pension figures or a second wage. A written pension estimate, honest hotel notice and a way to test a paid walking tour without risking Alma’s kitchen shifts would help. I cannot charge a guest for a story they never booked.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I enjoy showing people the old bridge. I do, but enjoying it is not a wage. I need a paid guest on the walking-tour sheet before I tell my wife Alma the walks can help with rent.

headlineQuote: I need a paid guest on the walking-tour sheet before I tell my wife Alma the walks can help with rent.
portrait: **Gareth**, 58, has competently managed hotel reservations for twelve years.
His bachelor’s degree, daily AI use and **average skill** sit beside low pay and under three weeks cash.
Alma’s **school-kitchen hours** vary, and few comparable hotel jobs are nearby.
He tests **prepaid bridge walks** without assuming visitors or his children will fund retirement.
Pension access and net income remain **unverified** across the horizons.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his bookings role before pension or paid walking demand is confirmed.
whatWouldHelp: A **written pension estimate**, honest notice and a safe paid tour test around Alma’s shifts would help.
